To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the FADS rs 174570 gene-diet interaction with long chain n- 3 PUFAs or fish intake was associated with long-term changes of BMI and body weight.
the FADS genetic variants interacted with long chain n- 3 PUFAs or fish intakes on long-term changes in body weight and BMI in four prospective cohorts.

the genetic associations of FADS rs174576 variant with long-term changes of BMI and body weight were accentuated by fish intake, and that the long chain n- 3 PUFAs were more strongly associated with changes in BMI among rs174576 T carriers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of fish and marine fatty acids in the development of obesity, and whether genetic factors may modify this relationship.
the interaction of fish and marine fatty acids (FA) intakes and FADS genotypes on long-term weight changes.
the interaction of fish and n-3 Pufa intakes with the genetic variants of the FADS gene cluster on long term BMI changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fish and marine fatty acids intake may interact with FADS genotype to affect long-term weight gain.

the interaction of FADS rs17457 genotype with fish and marine fatty acids on weight gain is not yet fully understood and further investigation is needed to fully confirm our findings in larger and other cohorts.
our findings are suggestive but not conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

fish and marine fatty acids intake, which are rich in long-chain n-3 Pufas, may interact with the genetic variant near FADS gene on long-term weight change, with potential implications for weight management.

the FADS rs274570 variant may be a marker for the long-term weight gain in the context of fish and n-3 Pufa-rich diets, which is in line with the evolutionary theory that the human FADS genes have been shaped by the dietary transition from fish and n- 3 PUFA-rich diet to plant and n-6 PUFA-rich diet.
the FADS variants interacted with n-3 PUFA intake on changes of BMI and that the interaction may be more pronounced among fish consumers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FADS genotype is an important factor to consider when assessing the effects of n-3 fatty acids on weight gain.
fish and marine fatty acids intake, the FADS genetic variants and their interaction may play a role in long-term weight gain and obesity.
the FADS genotype may help to identify individuals who would respond to n-3 PFA and fish interventions for weight loss.
